strengths: Synth-SBDH addresses a meaningful clinical NLP resource gap: 8,767 synthetic examples covering 14 SBDH categories plus pain, with spans, presence, temporality, and rationales. Its public availability and broader annotation coverage offer practical value.

The central utility claim has substantial empirical support. Synthetic pretraining improves several small models on two real clinical datasets; representative macro-F gains include 55.64 to 91.11 on MIMIC and 72.38 to 80.71 on VA data. Multiple architectures, three-run reporting, and low-resource experiments strengthen this evidence.

Expert review of all 1,755 original test examples is a substantial investment. Adjudication, corrected annotations, and detailed examples of omissions and unsupported inferences make the resource more useful and its limitations more transparent.

The appendix documents generation prompts, all 45 seed examples, filtering, category mappings, annotation guidelines, and training configurations. This documentation and the supported small-model classification benefits establish a contribution suitable for Findings.
weaknesses: The broader claims need qualification. Real-data experiments include supervised fine-tuning on each target dataset, MIMIC evaluation merges categories into four labels, and real-data NER is evaluated only on VA data. Encoder NER improvements are negligible, and several Mamba/Llama settings show no benefit. The evidence supports useful supervised adaptation more strongly than broad generalizability or consistently improved performance.

The experiments incompletely isolate why synthetic pretraining helps. Appendix D.2 usefully matches training steps against MIMIC pretraining, but category coverage and label balance differ. Rebalancing and seed-only baselines would clarify the contribution beyond these factors. The unusually unstable T5 baseline, with macro-F 25.44 ± 18.24, also makes its large relative improvement less persuasive as evidence of general extraction gains.

The strongest rare-category result concerns only 18 housing-insecurity test positives. Variation across three training runs does not quantify uncertainty from this small evaluation sample. Test-set confidence intervals would better support the headline 94.44-point improvement.

Evidence for reasoning distillation is limited. DSS improves macro-F by only 0.66 and 0.58 points, with the FLAN-T5 result nonsignificant (P=0.36), and evaluation remains within synthetic data. Extraction gains do not establish transferred reasoning capability. Real-data extraction evaluation would be possible without reference rationales at inference time.

The human evaluation is partly anchored to GPT-4: Appendix E.2 accepts a plausible category already chosen by GPT-4 while requiring a more specific category for newly added annotations. This makes reference labels partly dependent on the generator. Moreover, the 71.06% human alignment includes missing annotations in its denominator, whereas GPT-4 self-evaluation excludes them; those percentages are not directly comparable. Temporal prediction and explicit presence-attribute extraction also remain unevaluated.

Several reporting and reproducibility details need correction. Section 3.2's split counts sum to 8,727 rather than 8,767; Table 10 totals 14,369 annotations rather than 14,342. Table 14's Llama-3.2 baseline exactly repeats Table 3's ClinicalMamba means and standard deviations and should be verified. Exact classification prompts/verbalizers and GPT-4 sampling settings are not specified in the manuscript, while private VA data limits independent replication of the NER results.

The $90 versus $413,000 cost comparison does not provide comparable accounting for expert seed writing, synthetic-test annotation, adjudication, and validation. It supports inexpensive generation, but does not establish the reported magnitude of savings for producing equivalently validated resources.
